subject: checks-and-balances
title: Separation of Powers as Incentive Design
summary: Veto points, supermajorities, and the trade-off between stability and responsiveness.

cards.title: Org design for distrust
cards.text: A good operations leader designs controls assuming good people will sometimes err. The framers designed for officials who would sometimes abuse power. What does that look like in the actual mechanics?

cards.title: Incentives over virtue
cards.text: Federalist No. 51, one of the essays urging adoption of the Constitution: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition." The strategy was to give each branch both the means and the motive to resist encroachment.

cards.title: Supermajority thresholds
cards.text: Override of a veto needs two thirds of each House. Conviction on impeachment needs two thirds of senators present, and the penalty is capped at removal and disqualification from office. Treaties need two thirds of senators present. Thresholds encode how costly a mistake would be in each domain.
cards.example: Note the asymmetry: the House impeaches by simple majority, but conviction needs a Senate supermajority.

cards.title: An unwritten power
cards.text: Judicial review is not explicit in the text. The Supreme Court notes it was anticipated, including in the Federalist Papers, and confirmed in 1803 in Marbury v. Madison. One of the system's most consequential checks rests on interpretation and long practice, not an enumerated clause.

cards.title: The core trade-off
cards.text: More veto points means more stability and more protection against error or abuse. It also means more status quo bias and slower response. Defenders emphasize protection of rights and forced coalition-building. Critics emphasize gridlock, and that hard-to-pass laws can also be hard to fix.
cards.example: Neither view is partisan in itself. A useful self-test: would you value the brakes the same if the other side held power?

cards.question: How would you set the threshold for reversing a decision in your own organization? What would you require a supermajority for, and what should one person be able to decide?
nudges: Weigh the cost of a wrong action against the cost of a wrong inaction.
Is your view consistent no matter who holds the decision rights?

questions.q: What is the penalty limit for an impeachment conviction under the Constitution?

options.text: Removal from office and disqualification from future federal office
options.why: Right. Criminal prosecution is a separate process.
The Senate cannot imprison. The convicted person can still face ordinary prosecution.

options.text: A fine set by the House
options.why: Not a constitutional penalty for impeachment.
Not a penalty in the Constitution.

questions.q: Which check is not explicitly stated in the constitutional text?

options.text: Judicial review of the constitutionality of laws
options.why: Correct. Confirmed in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
Article I, Section 7 spells it out.

options.text: Senate advice and consent on judges

questions.q: What best describes the design logic of Federalist No. 51?

options.text: Align incentives so each branch's ambition checks the others
options.why: Yes: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
The essay assumes people are not angels.
No. No. 51 is about the internal structure of the national government.

sources.title: The Constitution of the United States: A Transcription
sources.supports: Veto override by two thirds of each House; the President shall "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed"; Senate advice and consent for judges; House impeaches, Senate tries, two-thirds to convict, judgment limited to removal and disqualification.

sources.title: The Federalist Papers: Text of Nos. 51–60
sources.supports: Federalist No. 51: "If men were angels, no government would be necessary" and "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."
